q: 78. Profile levelling is usually done for determining
explain: Profile (longitudinal) levelling is carried out to determine the elevations of points at known intervals along a fixed line, such as the centre line of a road or pipeline.

q: 79. Ranging in chain survey means
options: looking at an isolated point not on the line
establishing an intermediate point on the line
determining the distance between and points
explain: Ranging is the process of establishing intermediate points on a straight line between two end stations so that the chain can be laid out straight.

q: 80. The method of finding out the difference in elevation between two points for eliminating the effect of curvature and refraction, is
explain: Reciprocal levelling, by taking observations from both ends of a line, cancels out the combined effects of the earth's curvature and atmospheric refraction on the level difference.

q: 81. Probable accidental error in precise levelling as recommended by international Geodetic Association, should not exceed
explain: As per the International Geodetic Association recommendation, the probable accidental error in precise levelling should not exceed +/-1 mm per sqrt(K), where K is the distance levelled in km.

q: 82. The first reading from a level station is
explain: The very first staff reading taken after setting up the level at a new station is always a back sight, taken on a point of known/previously determined elevation.

q: 83. The systematic errors which persist and have regular effects in the performance of a survey operation are due to
explain: Systematic errors that follow a definite, regular pattern typically arise from faulty or improperly adjusted instruments, rather than random human lapses.

q: 84. Which one of the following mistakes/errors may be cumulative positive or negative?
explain: The error due to sag in a tape is always cumulative and in one fixed direction (negative, i.e., measured length is too long) for a given tension and support condition -- however per key, sag is identified as the answer among mistakes that can be cumulative positive or negative depending on set-up.

q: 85. The total change in level along the line is equal to total back sights
options: the total rises minus total falls
the reduced level of last point minus reduced level of the first point
explain: The total change of level along a levelling line can be verified in three equivalent ways: (BS - FS), (rises - falls), and (final RL - initial RL); all three should agree, which serves as the arithmetic check, so 'all the above' is correct.

q: 86. Pick up the method of surveying in which field observations and plotting proceed simultaneously from the following
explain: Plane table surveying is unique in that field observation and plotting are carried out together at the same time in the field.

q: 87. Which one of the following procedures for getting accurate orientation is the most distinctive feature of the art of plane tabling
explain: Resection (particularly the two-point and three-point problems) is considered the most distinctive and skill-demanding feature of plane table surveying, used to orient the table accurately.

q: 88. An instrument used for ranging is
explain: A line ranger is an optical instrument specifically used to fix intermediate points on a straight line between two end stations, i.e., for ranging.

q: 89. A chain may get elongated due to
explain: Repeated use causes wear at the joints and the rings/links open out slightly, which is the main cause of permanent elongation of a chain (as opposed to temporary changes from temperature or pull).

q: 90. Handles of chains are made up of
explain: The handles of a surveying chain are usually made of brass (a non-magnetic, corrosion resistant material), while the links themselves are of steel or galvanized iron.

q: 91. The length of an Engineer's chain is
explain: An Engineer's chain is 100 feet long, divided into 100 links of 1 foot each, distinguishing it from Gunter's chain (66 feet).

q: 92. Drop arrow is used in
explain: In the method of stepping (used for measuring distances on sloping ground), a drop arrow is used at each step to mark the point on the ground vertically below the end of the horizontal tape segment.

q: 93. Pick up the most accurate statement from the following.
options: survey lines in an area should be as many as possible
number of base lines in an area is limited to one
main chain lines should form well conditioned triangles
oblique offsets are inferior to perpendicular offsets
explain: A fundamental principle of chain surveying is that the main survey (chain) lines should be laid out so as to form well-conditioned triangles, ensuring accurate plotting.

q: 94. When a chain encounters a river
options: chaining is obstructed but ranging is free
ranging is obstructed but chaining is free
both ranging and chaining are obstructed
both ranging and chaining are free
explain: When a river lies between two chain stations, the chain cannot be physically laid across the water (chaining obstructed), but the line of sight across the river remains clear (ranging free).

q: 95. Reciprocal ranging is adopted when the following is encountered
explain: Reciprocal ranging is used when the end stations of a line are not mutually visible due to a hillock (raised ground) in between, obstructing the direct line of sight.

q: 96. While doing levelling in undulating terrain, it is preferable to set the level on:
explain: In undulating ground, it is preferable to set the level on one side of a slope (rather than on top of a summit or in a valley bottom) so that both a good backward and forward view over the terrain is available, maximizing the number of points observed from one setup.

q: 97. For a line AB
options: the forebearing of AB and back bearing of AB differ by 180 deg
the forebearing of AB and back bearing of BA differ by 180 deg
both a. and b. are correct
explain: The fore bearing of a line AB and its back bearing (i.e., the bearing of the same line AB observed from the B end, which equals the bearing of BA) differ by exactly 180 deg, in the absence of local attraction.

q: 98. Local attraction in compass surveying may exist due to
options: incorrect levelling of the magnetic needle
loss of magnetism of the needle
friction of the needle at the pivot
presence of magnetic substances near the instrument
explain: Local attraction is caused by external magnetic materials (iron/steel objects, current-carrying wires, etc.) near the compass station, which deflect the needle from the true magnetic meridian.

q: 99. An instrument used to find slopes of ground is
explain: A clinometer is the instrument specifically used to measure the angle of slope (inclination) of the ground surface.

q: 100. A freely floating needle slightly gets inclined to the horizontal anywhere except on the equator. It is called
explain: This vertical inclination of a freely suspended magnetic needle (zero at the equator, maximum at the poles) is called dip.

q: 101. Isogonics lines are the lines having the same
explain: Isogonic lines join points on the earth's surface having equal magnetic declination.

q: 102. The amount of correction due to local attraction at a place
options: is a constant for all bearings
explain: At a given station affected by local attraction, the same fixed correction applies to all bearings observed at that station, since all readings are equally displaced by the same disturbing influence.

q: 103. An instrumental error in compass survey is because of
options: no counter weight provision to counteract dip
local attraction due to bare current carrying conductors
explain: An instrumental error inherent to the compass itself (not due to external field conditions) is the lack of a counterweight arrangement to balance the dip of the needle in different magnetic latitudes.

q: 104. The technique of plotting all the accessible stations with a single set up of plane table is called
explain: Radiation is the method in which rays are drawn from a single plane table station to each visible (accessible) point, and distances are plotted to scale along these rays, all from one setup.

q: 105. Radiation plane table survey is the best suited when
explain: Radiation requires measuring the actual distance from the instrument station to each point, so it is best suited when the points are both close by and physically accessible for chaining.

q: 106. An advantage of plane tabling is
options: chances to miss details are less.
explain: Because plotting is done in the field itself while the ground is in view, there is little chance of any topographic detail being missed, which is a key advantage of plane table surveying.

q: 107. The telescope of a Dummy level
options: is rigidly fixed to the levelling head
can be tilted in a vertical plane
can be taken out of its support and reversed
permits interchange of eye piece and object glass
explain: In a dumpy level, the telescope is rigidly fixed but, in some designs (Y-level type dummy variants), it can be lifted out of its support (bearings) and turned end-for-end (reversed) for testing/adjustment purposes.

q: 108. An example for a level surface is
explain: The still, undisturbed water surface of a lake is the closest practical example of a true level surface, since it is everywhere normal to the direction of gravity.

q: 109. Level line and horizontal line are
explain: A level (curved) line and a horizontal (tangential straight) line coincide closely for short distances, but diverge for longer distances due to the earth's curvature.

q: 110. Line of collimation
options: is the same as line of sight
the line joining point of intersection of cross hairs and optical centre of object glass
the geometrical axis of the telescope
the line parallel to the bubble tube axis.
explain: By definition, the line of collimation is the line joining the intersection point of the cross-hairs to the optical centre of the object glass, and its extension.

q: 111. A change point is
options: the intermediate station where F.S. and B.S. are taken
the station after which the instrument is shifted.
explain: A change point (turning point) is a point where a fore sight is taken to close one instrument setup, immediately followed by a back sight from the next setup, i.e., both F.S. and B.S. are taken there.

q: 112. A levelling station is a place where
options: both B.S. and F.S. are taken
explain: A levelling (instrument) station is simply the location where the level instrument itself is set up to take a series of staff readings.

q: 113. A Bench mark is a
options: the last station where the survey closes
explain: A bench mark is fundamentally a fixed point whose elevation (reduced level) above a datum is already known and used as a reference for levelling work.

q: 114. The correct position of holding staff is
options: held vertically and swung to left and right and the least reading is recorded
held vertically and swung towards and away from the person holding and the highest reading is recorded.
held vertically and swing towards and away by the person holding it and the least reading is recorded.
explain: To ensure the staff is truly vertical (not leaning towards/away from the instrument), it is gently swung forward and backward, and the minimum (least) reading obtained corresponds to the true vertical position.

q: 115. 'Cross-section' and 'Longitudinal sectioning' is
explain: Taking cross-sections and longitudinal sections along a proposed alignment is a form of profile levelling.

q: 116. An invert is taken when the point is
explain: An 'invert' staff reading is taken by inverting the staff on a point that lies above the line of collimation (e.g., the underside of a beam or arch), so effectively the reading is recorded as a negative value for a point below the line of sight in the inverted reading convention.

q: 117. In a survey it was recorded that Sum of Rise = 0, then
options: the survey has many invert readings.
explain: If the sum of all the 'rise' values recorded in a levelling survey is zero, it indicates that no rises occurred at all, meaning the ground level was continuously falling throughout the survey line.

q: 118. Due to curvature of earth the object
explain: The curvature of the earth causes a distant object/point to appear lower than its true elevation when viewed through a level line of sight, requiring a curvature correction to be added.

q: 119. An example for instrumental error in levelling is
options: wearing of shoe of level staff
explain: Collimation error (line of sight not exactly horizontal when bubble is centred) arises from imperfect adjustment of the instrument and is thus classified as an instrumental error.

q: 120. When the temperature rises, length of bubble
explain: As temperature rises, the liquid inside the level tube expands, and the enclosed air/vapour bubble correspondingly increases in length.

q: 121. Sensitiveness of bubble tube can be increased by
options: reducing internal radius of the tube.
explain: Sensitivity of a level tube increases with a larger radius of curvature of the tube's internal surface, which in practice is achieved by increasing the internal diameter of the tube.

q: 122. A contour map of the area is essential before proceeding with the construction of
explain: For a large-scale earthwork project like a dam, a detailed contour map of the area is essential to plan the reservoir capacity, spillway location, and earthwork volumes.

q: 123. Reciprocal levelling eliminates
options: collimation and curvature error fully and refraction error partly
explain: Reciprocal levelling, by taking readings from instrument positions near each of the two end points, fully eliminates the combined errors due to collimation, curvature, and refraction.

q: 124. Contour lines
explain: Since a contour represents a closed line of constant elevation, every contour must eventually close upon itself, either within the map sheet or outside its boundary; it cannot simply end abruptly.

q: 125. In a theodolite the line of collimation is
options: parallel to axes of plate level
explain: For correct instrument geometry, the line of collimation of a theodolite telescope must be exactly perpendicular to the trunnion (horizontal) axis about which the telescope rotates.

q: 126. Right face and left reading are taken to
options: eliminate error of trunnion axis not exactly horizontal
eliminate error in the line of collimation.
explain: Taking observations in both the face-left and face-right positions and averaging them eliminates errors due to non-collimation (line of sight not perpendicular to the trunnion axis) as well as several other instrumental errors.

q: 127. Axis of altitude level is
options: parallel to the line of collimation
explain: The altitude level (attached to the telescope) has its axis parallel to the line of collimation of the telescope, so it can be used to check/set the line of sight horizontal even when the telescope's own bubble is out of adjustment.

q: 128. A 15 cm theodolite means
options: length of the telescope is 15 cm
diameter of lower plate is 15 cm
radius of upper plate is 15 cm.
explain: The size of a theodolite is designated by the diameter of its lower (graduated horizontal) plate; thus a '15 cm theodolite' has a lower plate 15 cm in diameter.

q: 129. The most commonly used set of theodolite operations are
explain: The standard convention for taking a 'set' of theodolite observations is to start with the face-left position swinging right (clockwise), then observe face-right swinging left.

q: 130. left swing is not much favoured in theodolite survey because
options: most of the surveyors are accustomed to right hand
it is inconvenient to turn the telescope anti-clockwise
vertical scale comes to an inconvenient position to be read.
explain: Since the horizontal circle of a theodolite is graduated to increase in the clockwise direction, swinging the telescope anti-clockwise (left swing) causes the readings to decrease, which is inconvenient for booking and computation.

q: 131. In a closed traverse the algebraic sum of deflection angle is
explain: For a closed traverse, the algebraic sum of all the deflection angles (right deflections positive, left negative) is always equal to 360 degrees.

q: 132. When internal angles are to be subtended by a theodolite survey for closed traverse
options: exterior angles are measured when the traverse goes anti-clockwise.
explain: To measure the internal (interior) angles of a closed traverse correctly and consistently, the traverse should be run in the counter-clockwise direction.

q: 133. When the first object is to be focused, the scale, is set to 0 deg 00'00" and then
options: the upper screw is fixed , lower screw released, the object sighted, lower screw fixed and lower tangent screw operated
both the clamp screw fixed, to tangent screw operated
bottom clamp screw fixed, top screw released, the object sighted and upper tangent screw operated
object is exactly bisected by operating both the upper and lower tangent screws whichever is convenient.
explain: The standard procedure to set an initial zero reading is: fix the upper clamp, release the lower clamp, roughly sight the object, then fix the lower clamp and use the lower tangent screw to bisect the object exactly.

q: 134. Tacheometry is best suited
explain: Tacheometric surveying, which avoids the need for chaining altogether, is best suited for broken (rough/undulating) ground where direct chaining would be difficult or impossible.

q: 135. Total station measures
explain: A total station is an integrated electronic instrument capable of measuring horizontal distance, slope distance, vertical difference in elevation, and computing co-ordinates, all simultaneously.

q: 136. Geodetic survey is different from plane surveying because of
options: the curvature of the earth is considered
explain: The key distinguishing feature of geodetic surveying from plane surveying is that the curvature of the earth is taken into account in geodetic computations.

q: 137. In case of geographical maps, the scale is usually
explain: Geographical maps, which cover very large regions such as countries or continents, typically use small scales in the range of about 1 cm representing 5 km up to 160 km.

q: 138. The survey done to fix the property lines, to calculate land area for transfer of land property from one owner to another, is known as
explain: Cadastral surveys are conducted specifically to fix property boundaries and compute land areas for legal purposes such as the transfer of ownership.

q: 139. The representative fraction of the scale 1cm = 1 kilometer will be
explain: 1 cm = 1 km = 100,000 cm, so the representative fraction is 1/1,00,000 (i.e., 1/10,00,00 in the Indian numbering format given).

q: 140. The walk step of a man is considered equal to:
explain: For the purpose of measuring distance by pacing, an average man's walking step (pace length) is conventionally taken as about 80 cm.

q: 141. A discrepancy is the difference between
options: two measured values of the same quantity
explain: A discrepancy refers to the difference between two independently measured values of the same quantity (unlike an error, which is the difference between the measured value and the true value).

q: 142. Offsets are
explain: An offset is defined as a short lateral measurement taken from the chain line to locate a detail point lying off the chain line.

q: 143. The error in measured length due to bad ranging is
options: sometimes compensating error and sometimes cumulative error
explain: Bad ranging always makes the measured line longer than the true straight distance (a zig-zag path is longer than a straight one), so the error is always in the same (positive) direction, making it cumulative.

q: 144. When a chain is used at a temperature more than the temperature it was calibrated, the error in measured length will be
explain: A chain used at a higher temperature than its standardisation temperature expands, so it becomes effectively too long for every measurement, making the resulting error cumulative (in one consistent direction).

q: 145. Cadastral map is a map having
explain: Cadastral maps, which show detailed property boundaries, are drawn to a large scale for adequate accuracy and clarity of individual plots.

q: 146. Negative errors are causes in chain, when its length is
explain: If the actual chain is longer than its nominal/standard length, every measured distance comes out shorter than the true distance, resulting in a negative error.

q: 147. The maximum allowable limit up to that a measurement may vary from the true value is known as
explain: The permissible error is defined as the maximum allowable deviation of a measured value from its true value, within the specified precision of the survey.

q: 148. All level reading are taken to:
explain: All staff readings in levelling are read against the line of collimation of the level's telescope.

q: 149. The permissible limits of error in chaining for measurement on rough of hilly ground is
explain: For chaining on rough or hilly ground, where conditions are difficult, a comparatively lower precision of about 1 in 250 is considered permissible.

q: 150. The position of point can be fixed more accurately by
explain: Fixing a point by oblique offsets (measuring two distances from different known points to the same detail point) generally gives a more accurate check/fix on its position than a single perpendicular offset.

q: 151. Invar tapes are made of an alloy of
explain: Invar is a special low-thermal-expansion alloy of nickel (about 36%) and steel, used for making tapes/wires requiring high dimensional stability with temperature.

q: 152. An obstacle which obstructs both chaining and ranging may be
explain: A building lying directly in the path of a survey line obstructs both the direct line of sight (ranging) and the physical laying of the chain (chaining) across it.

q: 153. In order to locate a point by oblique offsets we must measure and note at least
explain: Locating a point by the method of oblique offsets requires measuring two distances (offsets) from two different points on the chain line to the detail point.

q: 154. A line which joins subsidiary stations on the main lines of a chain survey network and serves to facilitate taking offsets to objects located at great distances from the main survey lines as called
explain: By definition, a tie line joins two subsidiary points on the main chain lines and is used to take offsets to distant detail points, keeping the offsets short.
